nameStory: The 'Fringed' part of this lichen's name comes from the delicate, hair-like projections called cilia that edge its lobes, creating a distinctly fringed appearance. The 'Wrinkle' refers to the characteristic ridged and furrowed surface texture that develops as this foliose lichen matures. It's like nature decorated a wrinkled leaf with tiny fringe trim!
description: Fringed Wrinkle Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms rosettes or irregular patches on tree bark, typically measuring 2-6 inches across. Its lobes are grayish-green when dry, turning more vibrant green when wet, with a distinctly wrinkled or ridged surface texture. The most striking feature is the fringe of tiny, dark hair-like projections (cilia) along the edges of each lobe. This medium-sized lichen creates attractive, circular to irregular colonies that can persist for decades on suitable host trees.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for distinctive ridges and furrows running across the surface, creating a wrinkled appearance like an old leather jacket. Run your finger gently across it - you'll feel the raised ridges and depressed valleys.

idTips.label: Fringe Features
idTips.description: The edges of the lobes are decorated with tiny, dark, hair-like projections (cilia) that create a distinct fringed border. These are easily visible with the naked eye and feel slightly bristly to the touch.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to blue-gray when dry, becoming brighter green when wet from rain or morning dew. The color change is quite dramatic and happens within minutes of getting wet.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms leafy, overlapping lobes that spread outward in rosette-like patterns. The lobes are moderately broad (about finger-width) and feel papery but flexible when dry.

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like maples and birches. Rarely found on conifers or rocks.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies typically span 2-6 inches across, though older specimens can reach nearly a foot in diameter. Each lobe is roughly 0.2-0.5 inches wide.

habitat: Fringed Wrinkle Lichen thrives on the bark of deciduous trees in New England's mixed hardwood forests, particularly favoring maples, birches, and occasionally oaks. It prefers partially shaded locations with good air circulation, often found in mature forest settings from sea level to moderate elevations. Look for it in areas with relatively clean air, as it's somewhat sensitive to air pollution.

seasonality.spring: Spring rains bring out the vibrant green coloration, making this an excellent time for photography and identification. The contrast between the bright green surface and dark fringe is most pronounced when wet.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, the lichen appears grayish and more subdued, but the diagnostic fringe and wrinkled texture remain clearly visible. This is when the papery texture is most apparent to touch.
seasonality.fall: Fall moisture from mist and rain reactivates the green coloration. The lichen stands out beautifully against autumn bark colors, making it easier to spot on tree trunks.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round, the lichen may accumulate snow on its surface. When exposed, it maintains its wrinkled texture and fringe, though colors remain muted in the dry winter air.

funFact: **[Uncertain claim flag]** This lichen can live for over 100 years, growing incredibly slowly at just a few millimeters per year - meaning that dinner plate-sized specimen you're admiring might have started growing before your great-grandparents were born!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other wrinkle lichens, but the distinctive dark fringe along the lobe edges is your best clue - remember 'fringe equals Fringed Wrinkle Lichen!' Other wrinkle lichens may have wrinkled surfaces but lack the prominent hairy border that makes this species unique.
contextualKnowledge: **[Uncertain claim flag]** This lichen is relatively uncommon in New England compared to its relatives, which explains the low observation count of only 8 recorded specimens. It may be overlooked by casual observers or confused with more common wrinkle lichens, making each sighting particularly noteworthy for citizen science projects.
compareHints: **[Uncertain claim flag]** Compared to Variable Wrinkle-lichen, Fringed Wrinkle Lichen has much more prominent and consistently present fringe hairs along its edges. Trailrunner tends to have longer, more numerous cilia, while Chestnut Wrinkle Lichen typically shows brownish coloration and less pronounced ridging. The combination of moderate-sized dark fringe and distinct surface ridging distinguishes Fringed Wrinkle Lichen from its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Variable wrinkle-lichen differs from its relatives by having the most pronounced wrinkled texture - fringed wrinkle-lichen has hair-like projections along edges, while trailrunner forms more elongated, strap-like lobes.
Trailrunner differs from its cousin Fringed Wrinkle Lichen by having more pronounced cilia and typically narrower lobes.
Unlike Fringed Wrinkle Lichen which has obvious hair-like projections along the edges, Chestnut Wrinkle Lichen has smooth lobe margins.
